utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Unfortunately, we have a late start due to the malfunctioning of the LiveNote system. Are you ready -- no, I have to look at the other side. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to continue the cross-examination of Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The great English phrase is, up to a point, Your Honour. The answer is yes, I am, subject to this, and it is a point to be raised before the witness comes into court in the first place. Your Honour knows that Mr. Kljuic was specifically asked to bring or to send in advance preferably material to which he had specifically referred in his, and it was a considerable quantity according to him of notes taken by him in the course of numerous meetings. Your Honour, the amount of material received from Mr. Kljuic so far is really very tiny indeed in relation to what he said. Now, Your Honour, he has been requested specifically by the Trial Chamber I think within the last week, from memory, but I think originally perhaps about a week ago or slightly less, perhaps, and then there was a follow-up communication which Your Honour has probably seen which attached a short note from me suggesting practicality which apparently was then helpfully adopted by the Trial Chamber. So Your Honour, I don't know at the moment what is the response and the reaction to that, and I don't know - and perhaps none of us knows without Mr. Kljuic being asked - what, if anything, he has brought to The Hague with him. So that's the starting point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you ask him, Mr. Stewart, and if there's any need of support by the Chamber, then we'll do that. As far as the number of pages, he indicated at that time it was at least -- by rereading the matter it was not entirely clearly whether that would be only of the relevant period, that is the period covered by the indictment, because the couple of hundred pages he talked about was, as far as I remember, over a larger period. But you may ask him. And Mr. Usher, could you escort Mr. Kljuic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your response, I understand that you do hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Keeping in mind, Mr. Kljuic, the reasons why you are not at all times available over the last couple of weeks or month, I'm glad to see you as far as I can see but that's just the amateur's eye in good health. Welcome back in court, Mr. Kljuic. Mr. Kljuic, on the 27th of September, 2004, you have made a solemn declaration that you would speak the truth -- that you would tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. I'd like to remind you not only of the fact that you made the solemn declaration but also of the text of it, which I just pronounced, and I'd like to remind you that in the examination that will follow, you're still bound by that solemn declaration. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kljuic. Mr. Kljuic, did you receive in the course of the last week or ten days a communication in relation to -- a communication from The Hague in relation to the bringing by you, or sending by you to The Hague of material which might be relevant to this case?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't receive any communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kljuic. Your Honour, that's a very unsatisfactory start, is it not, I ask rhetorically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kljuic, at the end of the hearing on the 29th of September last year, you were invited to send to us and to bring with you upon your return the notes you had made. We received some of it through the Victims and Witnesses Unit. There was a limit number of notes. Did you bring remainder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I told Mr. Stewart that I had some notes, I also told him that I did not keep a diary in any serious manner but that periodically, I made note of some details that I believed were significant at that time. I sent you some material that, in part, was typed out and in part was in handwriting. I have brought here with me some other texts from 1990, 1992, 1995, and these are indeed contemporaneous documents from the period, and I have also taken a copy of the material that I sent to you. However, my luggage has been lost during my journey; I'm expecting it to be delivered to me. I also have to tell you that in -- while writing my book on Bosnia, and I will convey to you what the structure of the book is tomorrow when my luggage arrives, then you will see which parts are relevant because as I was completing some chapters, I was going through the written documentation. Therefore, whatever I was able to send over to you, I did, whatever I believed would be of interest to you. For the rest, what is contained in my testimony, I still adhere to that and of course you are welcome to ask further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kljuic, the problem is that this court, this Chamber would like to make its own assessment of what is relevant and to some extent, of course, one could accept, perhaps, that material from 1994 would be -- especially if it deals with contemporaneous issues, that it might not be that relevant, although sometimes people are looking back in 1994 to what happened in 1992, so it's not under all circumstances irrelevant. So I do understand that you have got the material with you but it's temporarily lost with your luggage. Could you tell us what -- but briefly, if you say the other material what was not relevant, I mean of course we have seen the material you brought which is certainly not complete and very much are personal impressions rather than anything else. Could you tell us on the basis of what you thought the other material, and let's concentrate on material from 1991, 1992, why that was not relevant? I mean what type of material did you exclude from your relevance test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not radically exclude anything, I simply had some items and I didn't have others. However, when I will present the structure of my book to you, which I will do tomorrow, you will see that the book contains 16 chapters, starts with the fall of the Berlin Wall and ends with the trial before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you came - and we are quite happy you came - to answer questions. If one of the questions would be about the structure of a book that has not yet been published, you are invited to answer that question, but this is not a place to present an overall view but this is a place, rather, where you give answers to the questions of the parties and questions of the Bench. But do I understand that you have got all the material brought with you? Would you mind if it would be copied if it's here, once it has been retrieved, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I haven't brought all the material, only some fragments. I don't know what -- where your interest lies. On the other hand, I don't have all of the material. I only have parts that I made note of, that I took press clippings of, and it is just an overview of the times in which we lived. So what I can do is I can make a photocopy of all the material I have. What I do not know, however, is what you're interested in. I was compiling material for my book and not, of course, for the purposes of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, that's exactly the reason why we asked you to bring and to send everything so that we could assess what would be relevant or that the parties could assess what was relevant. But I do understand that you do not mind if photocopies are made tomorrow of the material which I brought, although it still has to be retrieved. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask for the witness to leave court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kljuic, could you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether to laugh or cry, frankly. Your Honour, this is a deeply unsatisfactory situation, but I do have an immediate practical suggestion which is this, and I've made contingency plans Your Honour because I foresaw this sort of difficulty. Your Honour, my proposal is I can get Ms. Loukas here at very short notice, that the court proceeds with Mr. Omeragic's evidence, I understand that the Prosecution are ready to proceed with Mr. Omeragic. Ms. Loukas is ready to proceed with Mr. Omeragic, all I've got to do is ask her to get here from not very far away quite quickly. Your Honour, we must have, with respect, Mr. Kljuic's material. We must have his luggage and we must have the opportunity of exploring this. It is quite impossible to consider that it's right to proceed with Mr. Kljuic until we sorted this out. This was the part of the very -- it was the very thing, as Your Honour has indicated, it was the very thing that Mr. Kljuic was asked and has been consistently asked to do. He has plainly, without even any exploration, in questioning of him, he has plainly signally failed to do what is clear he should do, and this material is potentially important. Because he doesn't produce it, we don't know how important, but it is certainly impossible to discard it as not being potentially of very great significance to his evidence and his cross-examination. So My Lord -- Your Honours, that's my practical suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know if we're ready to proceed with Mr. Omeragic or if he's even in the building at this point in time so I'm making an inquiry right now. It seems to me, there is another solution and that is that we proceed as best we can with Mr. Kljuic's continued cross-examination tomorrow when he produces the information to the Court and to the parties. It can be he reviewed, and should Mr. Kljuic be required to come back, I'm quite sure he would come back. We can make that inquiry of Mr. Kljuic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had understood -- I had understood from what inquiries I've been able to make that everybody had assumed that Mr. Omeragic might come on quite soon, everybody was ready, but I can understand that just as we have to physically get people here, the Prosecution may face the same issue. But, Your Honours, going to the other issue: Your Honour, it is simply not practically possible to proceed with Mr. Kljuic's cross-examination in two stages; one in the absence of the very material he was invited to bring; and then to review that material and carry on. That is absolutely not the right way to proceed with a serious cross-examination of a really quite important witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will take one or two minutes to consider the situation. I've got one question for you, Mr. Stewart. If that material arrives, let's just assume that it would arrive this afternoon, what, then, after we have dealt with Mr. Omeragic, what would then be the programme?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to some extent, I've got to say, that depends on the material but when the material arrives, we will, as we have done already with the material which he provided, we will review it, and we includes of course such B/C/S speaker as we have on the team, we will review it as speedily as possible, Your Honour, and then I will -- I would then proceed with whatever areas of cross-examination first thing tomorrow morning, I could proceed with in the light of that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Another short question: Would you agree with me that what we have seen until now is material which mainly consists of very personal impressions hardly containing any facts, very incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, broadly speaking yes, which is precisely my complaint because what we have is a tiny amount of material, we have no idea how that -- how representative that is of the material that Mr. Kljuic has got and no idea of what questions might arise out of what has got lost on the way, apparently, in relation to anything else he's got. Your Honour puts your finger, in effect, on what is very much an element of our very complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter for one moment. --- Break taken at 10.03 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber has considered the present situation. There was no order for the witness to bring, there was a request for the witness to bring his material. He did send a smaller part and made it available to the parties. The Chamber, although it's not in evidence, has seen it and also gained the impression that it was material which very much reflected personal impressions rather than anything else. The witness is invited to make available to the parties what he has brought, and from what I understand he's willing to do so. That material, again, is not in evidence. We hope that it arrives soon for the parties. If at any later stage the Defence, on the basis of that material, would consider it necessary to further cross-examine the witness, we'll consider that at that moment if a motion is filed whether oral or written motion but at this moment, the Defence is given an opportunity and invited to cross -- further cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- may I ask for a certificate to appeal that ruling under 73(B).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a shocking decision, Your Honour, and we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stewart, you may ask for a certificate. You are not allowed to comment in these words on the decision taken by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, it was my submission; I withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you escort Mr. Kljuic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, what is the answer, please to my application for a certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that most likely during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The only thing is that I need to know because if I am to appeal the matter -- the witness should leave court, Your Honour, and not have been brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Stewart, the situation is a 73(B) certificate, is a certificate, we will decide on it. It has no --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just immediately saying the witness shouldn't be brought into court in the middle of these submissions. That's my immediate point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as a matter of fact, you started making submissions when the witness is brought into court. Mr. Kljuic, would you have one more minute of patience and follow the usher again. We have, unfortunately, I might have been a bit early to ask you back into court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The only problem with it is this, Your Honour, that an appeal on a matter like this is really -- the word we always use in England is nugatory, but much of the point of an appeal in relation to a matter like this is completely removed if, pending the resolution of the matter, one has to proceed anyway. So Your Honour, I would invite the Trial Chamber at least to tell me whether my application for a certificate under 73(B) is granted or refused because then I know where I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you say you make your application, you'd like to have a decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then absence of any reasons underlying your request for a certificate, it is denied --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, you have not invited me to give any reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I haven't been given an opportunity. Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't say I wasn't giving any reasons because I haven't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart, you insisted on an answer on a motion which consisted just of one line and that is you wanted a certificate. I then said: "Was that your motion? Was that all?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's quite true that I simply asked for an answer. But, Your Honour, I am asking for a brief opportunity to give reasons, and to shut me out from giving reasons on the basis of what, in this extremely unusual situation, to hold me to what I've said on the transcript as if it was some sort of legislative provision, Your Honour, is not, with respect, a fair way of dealing with it. I do wish to suggest reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber gives you an opportunity to file in writing the reasons for your certificate you asked, and the Chamber sees no reason at this moment to discontinue the proceedings in respect of the cross-examination of Mr. Kljuic. So therefore, although a decision has been given, we'll not take that as the final moment. You didn't give any reasons, but if you intend to give any reasons, you may file them in writing and we'll then consider whether those reasons should lead to a decision that a certificate will be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can give the reasons in less than two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart, you will not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the public would then know what the reasons were and we could have dealt with it. And Your Honours would be in a position to rule then at the earliest possible opportunity, because I can't deal with the written submissions until the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, we'll now continue with the cross-examination of the witness and we'll -- during the next break, we'll consider whether you will be given two minutes to give your reasons. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged for that, Your Honour. May I make one practical request while the witness is coming into court. If I were to give somebody Ms. Loukas's number, I wonder if somebody could bring and try to prevent her from making an unnecessary journey now and head her off, so she can continue what she was working on. That would be a favour, if anybody was able to get a hold of her which I can't right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Philpott offers to contact Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's very kind, Your Honour. Because I'm sure Your Honour will appreciate that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You anticipated that matters would take a different course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I made contingency plans so I could be as helpful as possible to the Court, Your Honour. That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you can escort Mr. Kljuic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I was just explaining to Ms. Philpott, we do not have people in the Defence room at the moment. We just don't have anybody else in the building apart from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any mobile phone on which Ms. Loukas could be reached?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, am I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- Ms. Philpott gets the assistance of my secretary in order to reach Ms. Loukas on her mobile phone in order to inform her.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm obliged for that. That is certainly helpful to the use of Defence resources. Your Honour, my first question, with respect -- excuse me, Mr. Kljuic, may I address it to Your Honour, is am I permitted this morning to pursue any questions in relation to the material or non-provision of material or the circumstances in relation to the material which was discussed at the previous hearing and has been under some consideration this morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may ask ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not object to such questions. Of course I do not know what the position of the Prosecution is. Also I'd like to -- you to keep in mind a few words I said about the position of a witness in this respect in bringing the material. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I don't have in mind this morning -- perhaps I also communicate this to you with respect to Their Honours, I don't have in mind to conduct some extensive exploration of what notes and what material you have, given that there is some material in a suitcase that hasn't found its way here, so any such detailed exploration I will reserve until having had a chance to look at that. But may I ask you simply as a practical matter, the -- there's a lost suitcase, is there, that you checked in in Sarajevo, did you, that hasn't arrived in The Hague. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My luggage was lost en route from Vienna to Amsterdam. I did not receive any written request to submit more material except for what I already submitted to your administration in Sarajevo, but I did bring along this part so that I could respond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, on this practical matter, it would be helpful if you could just specifically deal with what I'm asking. It seems to come to the same thing. You checked in a bag at Sarajevo, you flew via Vienna and apparently -- is it a suitcase or more than one suitcase has got mislaid between Vienna and Amsterdam. Is that the current situation?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a suitcase, exactly, that is the situation, one suitcase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have reported it in the usual -- it is the usual way unfortunately with the particular airline which I guess you travelled with. You have reported it in the usual way to the airline and the baggage handlers ...

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have all the usual bits of paper with reference numbers on; correct? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What has the airline said to you or the people responsible for baggage delivery, what have they said to you about the expectation of delivery of your bag?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that they would do everything in their power to find it, to locate it, and perhaps they have already located it, so it will be here on the next flight of Vienna. That is what they told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You haven't been told so far that it's been located; that's what I understand. You haven't been told that they have located it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't been told. But the woman who is in charge of me, the lady at the hotel. Said that it was -- they are going to find it and that it is being dealt with properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, did you bring any papers that might be of any possible relevance to this case in your hand luggage?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe that that is relevant for this -- for these proceedings. I have brought some of my notes by way of illustrations, and I have brought fragments of my book that have already been finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgot about the book for the moment, and not dismissive of it at all, Mr. Kljuic, except for immediate purposes, forget about the fragments of your book. So far as the other material is concerned which you did bring in your hand luggage, first of all, what is the quantity of that material, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: All told, with what I have already submitted to you, it's perhaps 100 pages. Actually, I submitted 37 pages to you before and there is another quantity, up to 100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's about 60 pages -- it doesn't matter to 10 or 15, it's about 60 pages or something like that, is it?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't counted, but yes, I guess that is more or less so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you frequently shrug your shoulders in answer to my questions. May I simply remind you that the only person who has firsthand knowledge of this is you which is why I'm asking the questions. The -- so Mr. Kljuic, this 60-odd pages, this is -- this does not include the draft chapters of your book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to clarify one thing first. You are asking me what the number of pages is. I did not count the number of pages in Sarajevo nor did you ask me to. So now I can only tell you approximately and you want me to tell you -- you don't want me to tell you precisely the number. In fact, I'm not sure what it is that you are asking me to do. I have given you my notes for your inspection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, please, what I'm asking you to do is specifically what I asked in my question. I asked you for an estimate of the amount of material. You have given an estimate. I have not pressed you for any more detail. I have accepted your estimate for the moment. And then I'm simply asking you of that 60-odd pages that you estimate, I'm simply asking you whether that -- those papers exclude draft chapters of your book. That's the only question I'm asking right now, please.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They also contain excerpts from my book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, how many pages have you brought which are not draft passages of your book but which are the kind of notes as you've sent them before, the type of notes, handwritten or typed out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you sent us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And I have taken along a copy for me, for my use. And also another -- I have taken along another number of pages, but I don't know what number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much additional pages did you bring apart from what you've sent us of a similar nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not of the same nature; it is of a different nature. It is about different developments, different events. I cannot tell you the exact number of pages because I have not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm speaking into the microphone. Can you hear me now? I'm speaking into the microphone. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do read your transcript, the answer was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The interpreter was asking whether we can hear her --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking because the microphone of the interpreter is on and I did the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought was happening, Your Honour. Because I could hear her, that was -- naturally, it follows from what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did everyone receive English translation. Am I the only one who did not receive it or... Mr. Stewart, did you receive an English translation of the last answer of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I got to, "I cannot tell you the exact number of pages because I am not," and the interpreter asked her question as to whether we were hearing her. So the answer then of course has finished so far because the interpreter raised that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the lines on page 18 and following, where the witness answers the question, did you hear that or...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it down to "because I have not ..." That was what happened and then the answer got broken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a problem, it seems. Could you speak a few words?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you hear me now? Can you hear me now? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is better without hearing sometimes what you say yourself. It seems to be better now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you. I'm afraid it was a problem of my earphones. Now I have to reread it. You said the additional material was not of the same nature because it dealt with different subjects. When I said "of the same nature" I meant to refer to the type of notes, that is, handwritten or typed out personal impressions. How many pages of this type of material you would have brought, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure, but there is more than the number of pages that I submitted to you previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do you have any idea, is that 20 or 50 additional pages or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say, Your Honour. I really can't say. I'll bring this file tomorrow and I'll show it to you once my suitcase comes. I haven't counted it because I really did not expect this type of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be willing to give it to the Victims and Witness Unit even before tomorrow, as soon as your suitcase has been retrieved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. The moment it arrives, you will get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm a little confused, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, before that practical interjection, I had been asking you about the material that you have brought with you and have got here in The Hague in your hand luggage, and you referred to 37 pages which seemed to be a completely different 37 pages. But Mr. Kljuic, I was really trying to get from you of the 60-odd pages that you say you actually have got here in The Hague, how much of that is not draft chapters of your book?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Stewart. It is not true that I have anything in The Hague. I had to sleep in my shirt, and I did not change my suit because everything except my glasses and my phone is in my baggage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I asked you absolutely specifically about five, ten minutes ago, specifically if you had got papers with you in your hand luggage. Your hand luggage wasn't mislaid on the way, was it?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, it wasn't. But only the telephone, my drugs and my glasses are in my hand luggage. Everything else is -- was in the suitcase, and I have come here without my suitcase. I checked into my hotel in this suit and here I am in this suit today. So no papers whatsoever were in my hand baggage, hand luggage. I only had my drugs, my medicaments, my telephone and my glasses. At the moment the suitcase is found, however, of course, the person, whoever wants to, whoever is in charge, can have all my papers. There's no reason why that shouldn't be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, one moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you Mr. Kljuic, page 16, line 16: "Mr. Kljuic, did you bring any papers that might be of any possible relevance to this case in your hand luggage?" You said: "I do not believe that that is relevant for this -- for these proceedings. I have brought some of my notes by way of illustrations, and I have brought fragments of my book that have already been finished." I said: "Forget about the book for the moment, not dismissive of it at all except for immediate process, forget about the fragments of your book. So far as the other material that is concerned that you did bring in your hand luggage, what is the quantity of that material roughly speaking?" And you answered: "All told with what I have already submitted to you, it's perhaps 100 pages. Actually, I submitted 37 pages to you before, and there is another quantity up to 100." And then I sought to clarify whether you meant there was 100 in addition to 37 or the balance of the 100 after we had taken away the 37. But I do suggest it was very clear at that point that I was asking you about hand luggage. I just want to get it straight now, Mr. Kljuic. You said a moment ago that you did not have any papers in your hand luggage. So, please, which -- just to be clear now, not forget, but -- we're moving forward rather than into the past.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the position? Have you brought any papers in your hand luggage that are now in The Hague? Please.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. My hand luggage is, in fact, here in the waiting room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this right, then: That the 100 pages that you were talking about, first of all, includes -- I understand it's not exact, Mr. Kljuic. The 100 pages includes the 37 pages that have already been submitted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The numbers may not be exact by the point you agree with; is that what we're saying?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the number of pages that is in the lost -- sorry, mislaid - I hope they'll find it for you, Mr. Kljuic - the number of pages that is in the mislaid suitcase is somewhere around 60; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, did you -- I sound like a work for an airline. Did you pack your suitcase yourself?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did pack the administrative and the male part, as it were. And the underwear and the rest was packed by my wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody else give you any papers to bring with you to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's your personal estimate of your own papers that you put into the suitcase, it's around 60-something pages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, Mr. Stewart has asked you how many pages there were approximately. You said about 100, including the 37 you already gave to us. What makes you say that it's probable or it's possible that 60 are new? Because most people that deduct 37 from 100 would come to 63, approximately 60. What makes you so cautious?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I don't know the precise number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The probable and the possible is -- might not have been necessary because, Mr. Stewart, you expressed yourself in terms of approximate, of around. Let's, before we come to, I suspect, the socks of Mr. Kljuic, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, leaving socks aside, I'm just not sure, apart from the act that it's pretty obvious everybody could do with one, but I'm not sure what the Tribunal has in mind as far as a break now is concerned, given the rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had a late start, so if you would say this would be a suitable moment for you for a break then we would adjourn until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's as suitable as any, Your Honour. So if it suits the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until five past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, Mr. Stewart, it is not my pleasure but for the completeness of the transcript, it's necessary that I repeat what my decision was on your application for a certificate because I was interrupted before it was translated and transcribed. So the decision was that your request was turned down. We promised you that you would know whether or not and when and whether oral or in writing you would get an opportunity to give the reasons for your application. You said you could do it in two minutes. You have two minutes from now on -- to give the reasons for your oral application, but if you'd prefer to do it in writing of course, you are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour what I have done is I have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. Over the break, I have prepared written reasons. May I simply supplement them with what might be less than two minutes of just a couple of points of explanation. May I do that straight away, Your Honour, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. As far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Within the time limit set, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Starting now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Point number one I have in mind particularly what the Trial Chamber said this morning at page 9, lines 22 to 20-something 23-27, but the next few lines, Your Honours's characterisation, it's page 9, line 18, I think, something like that, and then those next few lines. Secondly, number two, look at the transcript of the last occasion when Mr. Kljuic was here will make that good. Thirdly, the failure by the Tribunal in which I include the different arms of the Tribunal because after all, the Defence is relying on the Trial Chamber, the Victims and Witnesses Unit. It was out of our hands, and we were assured it would be taken care of, and it clearly hasn't been. The communication has been late and has not got through to Mr. Kljuic. So far as the rest of the matters are concerned, Your Honour, I don't think there's anything that I can add. Just to say overall that of course these do not constitute refined grounds of appeal. They've been knocked out in about 10 minutes over the break as the basis for a certificate, so of course we would reserve our position. But, Your Honour, it is, we submit, important that this is clearly a matter of interlocutory appeal. It's absolutely pointless if it's left until final, and as an interlocutory appeal, it is also, we submit, pointless if Mr. Kljuic's evidence proceeds for any material time. Point number 9 does seem to be the position. We brought Ms. Loukas here. She got all the way here but she had to go all the way back again, but thank you for the attempts -- or the successful attempts to contact her. But on balance, Your Honour, we submit that there was no possible reason why Mr. Omeragic's evidence couldn't have proceeded. It wouldn't have inconvenienced anybody and in fact would have been a help to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Then one final, but this is just in order to assist you, we spent a lot of time on relevant pages of approximately 60 in hand luggage. I, of course, ask myself why this went wrong. At least there were two questions and one you asked about relevant material in the hand luggage. Apart from that I do understand the hand luggage in English or cabin luggage is not exact -- but let's stay away from that. The witness answered to your question on the relevance of, it seems, all material he thinks he has. There were clearly two questions in one which caused a lot of confusion. Therefore, I think in general terms, dealing with one issue in one question saves us a lot of confusion. This is just to assist you, because I think you find it a pity that you couldn't use your time and have this clarified immediately instead of spending so much time on it, and so does the Chamber. So I think we have a shared interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I certainly did, Your Honour. I certainly accept the basic principle throughout the case that as far as possible, two questions in one should be avoided. I will, perhaps Your Honours will understand not as an absolute top priority, because I shall look at what I did this morning to see whether my technique in eliciting simple answers to simple questions in that sort of area can be improved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Kljuic may be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply say before Mr. Kljuic comes in that I am going to invite Your Honours' very firm assistance, may I put it this way, in improving Mr. Kljuic's technique in giving a straight answer to a straight question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I feel this as an encouragement to -- not to wait too long to intervene if the answers do not come.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think Your Honour has correctly understood a very important element of my ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suppose the strict technical position is that I am still awaiting Your Honours' ruling, strictly speaking, on my application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have now -- let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's obviously all three of Your Honours will need the opportunity of reviewing my reasons as set out on the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I first ask the Prosecution whether they take any position on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll read what you have written down and -- what you have submitted in writing and what you have added orally, and we'll give a decision after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, Mr. Stewart will continue to cross-examine you. May I direct you to carefully listen to the question and to focus, in your answer, exactly on what was asked. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljuic, I suppose I should ask: Any news from the airline front over the last half an hour about your bag?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none. But the lady who is waiting for me in the waiting room told me that they were going to sort this thing out today. And of course I kindly asked the staff here to assist me once I get hold of my luggage to go and have photocopies made of the material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Kljuic, I -- it seems an obvious common sense thing to do which I'm sure you have in mind, but you will follow this up as best you can with the airline or whatever appropriate contact numbers you've been given during the next break, will you? Did you hear me, all right? The microphone's been ...

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't really been the one doing this but rather the escort from the Victims and Witnesses Section. He met me there, and he said he was going to take care of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask Madam Registrar to send an additional message to the Victims and Witness Section that whenever there's any news about the luggage that we'll be informed, and first of all that the witness gets it as soon as possible and that copies are made on the request of the request of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I just supplement that, Your Honour, by request, with respect, that the Victims and Witnesses Unit take the utmost care to ensure that this matter doesn't fall between two stools, with somebody thinking that Mr. Kljuic is to contact the airline Mr. Kljuic thinking that somebody else is going to. This is -- this is a matter of considerable practical importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is included.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And I'm sure Mr. Kljuic heard that and the Victims and Witnesses Unit will be hearing it or will understand it as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you did not meet Mr. Krajisnik during the pre-election campaign in 1990, did you?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you really, but I believe that perhaps on the occasion when we were meeting, and when I say "we" I mean the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ, our paths might have crossed. I cannot tell you though precisely, I only know that the communication between these parties was a very intense one at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And such occasions on which you spoke to Mr. Krajisnik in 1990 and 1991 were mainly by accident in passing between a deputy and somebody who was himself a deputy and the president of the Assembly. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not accidental encounters. The two of us were discharging high officials -- high officers. Mr. Krajisnik was Speaker of the Assembly and I, myself, was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia. These were, therefore, posit meetings either in the Assembly or in the Presidency or on the occasion of formal meetings with representatives of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army and representatives of the international community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you described Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik as having been friends. But what do you know, Mr. Kljuic, from your own firsthand knowledge which supports the view which you have expressed that they were very close in politics?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was obvious to all, their positions in the setting up of the SDS party and in the operation of the SDS party were the leading ones. Besides, even before, they were working together in a process that I do not wish to speak of here, but they were together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know, Mr. Kljuic, then, about Mr. Krajisnik's work in the setting up of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that everybody was under the impression that the main office or rather the central figure of the party was Mr. Krajisnik because of his seriousness, his approach to the work, unlike Mr. Karadzic who was more of a spokesperson who liked to appear in public. These were the impressions that we got as we were participating in politics, but also this was the way they were perceived by the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, just I hope a one-sentence introduction to my next question. You have, on many occasions in giving evidence before this Trial Chamber, answered questions by referring to the way in which somebody was seen by the public, the impression given. I want to make it clear my question there in asking you what you know about Mr. Krajisnik's work in the setting up of the SDS party, that is one question; it means exactly what it says. I'm not asking you to tell us about others' impressions. I'm asking you to tell the Trial Chamber what you, Mr. Kljuic, know.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Krajisnik was the driving force of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know, Mr. Kljuic, please.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you the following: On the occasion of interparty meetings, there would be several representatives participating in these meetings on behalf of the Serb side; like for instance, Ms. Biljana Plavsic, the late Professor Koljevic, one Dukic from Han Pijesak. These meetings were efficient and valid only if they were also attended by Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what point in time does the answer that you've just given apply?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This applies to the period in advance of the elections. I mean the period in which we were developing as peoples' parties before the elections. The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina comprised seven members: Two Serbs, two Croats --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, just for the moment, I'm going to ask you not to take us into the composition of the Presidency and stick with what I'm asking you. The elections were in November 1990, we know that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When do you recall the SDS party being established?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was established in late spring or early summer. First, the SDA was established in May, and then the SDS followed suit in June, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or July?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Or July maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meetings that you have described a moment ago, then, the interparty meetings where there would be several representatives participating in these meetings on behalf of the Serb side, like, for instance, Mrs. Plavsic and so on, are you talking about meetings that took place between July 1990 and November 1990?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first meetings were not attended by Ms. Plavsic but rather by Mr. Karadzic. However, these meetings were very frequent in the period between August and November. There's one detail concerning the agreement that is very significant that I wanted to talk about just a moment ago when you interrupted me. There was the tendency to change the structure of the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, is what you're about to say an answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I wanted to tell you where we had the decisive support of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. This is just an illustration of the case if you want to hear it. If not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kljuic. The question was whether you were talking about meetings between July 1990 and November 1990. You answered that question by saying that it was frequent in the period August to November. So the time frame which Mr. Stewart was asking for has been answered. If he wants to know other matters, he'll ask you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you talked earlier about Mr. Krajisnik's role in the setting up of the SDS, you agree that must be talking about a period before July 1990?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what do you, Mr. Kljuic, know about Mr. Krajisnik's role in the setting up of the SDS before July 1990?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I wasn't particularly interested in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very nice, Mr. Kljuic, but what is the answer to the question then? Does it follow because you weren't interested, the answer is you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. know nothing?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know because we perceived him as one of the founders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic. Mr. Kljuic. Mr. Stewart is asking you what knowledge you have about the role of Mr. Krajisnik prior to the date where the SDS was established. If you say, "We perceived," tell us what you observed that made you believe that. Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SDS gathered a large number of eminent Serbs. Once their convention was held, it was reported about in a newspaper called Javnost. From these papers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did -- were conventions held before the party was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The convention was taken as the date of the official establishment of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you observe about what Mr. Krajisnik did or -- well, what his role was before that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is why evidently he was the central figure: From each party, we would pick out an operative, so to speak, who would prepare certain -- a certain position paper. I chose Mr. Tomislav Obrdalj from the HDZ. There was Amila Omersaftic on behalf of the SDA, and they often went to see Mr. Krajisnik to coordinate their views and positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are talking now about party activities. The question was before the party was established. So what did Mr. Krajisnik do before the convention held in July before the party was established? What did you see him -- did he send the invitations? Did he draft the statutes? Did he appear on television and announce that such a thing would happen? What did you see, what made you believe that he was such an important person in that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While Karadzic talked about political matters to a larger extent, Mr. Krajisnik was definitely the person who worked on the party's documents because that is also how he made his public addresses. Whatever he talked about at the time was very acceptable because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say he was definitely the one who worked on the documents. Could you give an example of that? Could you tell us about a document you know he worked on and tell us how you know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the establishment, I don't know which documents he worked on; probably on the Statute. But Mr. Karadzic did not regard this with a favourable eye. Later on when he was -- later on as Speaker of parliament, Mr. Krajisnik worked on all the key documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you should be aware that Mr. Stewart is asking you about that period before July. You say, "He probably worked on the Statute, but Mr. Karadzic did not regard this with a favourable eye." What do you know -- how do you know that he worked on the Statute of the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I definitely know that Karadzic did not and there was nobody else. Mr. Krajisnik was the most suitable person for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he was suitable; Karadzic didn't do it; no one else could have done it; so therefore it must have been Krajisnik. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose so. I cannot claim with any certainty. This was a period of time when I was not yet interested in seeing how they worked. It was later on when Krajisnik became Speaker of the parliament that I became interested in him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. What Mr. Stewart did is he tested, more or less, your testimony on the role of Mr. Krajisnik in setting up the SDS party. This Chamber is aware that sometimes conclusions and observations come close to each other but we'd rather hear facts, observations, than, I would say, impressions or conclusions. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed. At the same time, setting up, of course, is a -- the ambiguity of setting up is at least from my understanding of the English could be establishing, setting up, making something function. But I leave that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, two comments on that, Your Honour. One is the phrase came from the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Secondly, actually although -- well, I'm reasonable expert at the English language now, Your Honour, there's very ambiguity in the phrase "setting up" in this context, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Harmon would suggest some startling ambiguity in the same phrase. They speak a similar language to us on his side of the Atlantic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you said that Mr. Krajisnik -- I'm sorry, Dr. Karadzic did not view favorably, I think, was your phrase. You said: "Mr. Krajisnik probably worked on the Statute but Mr. Karadzic did not regard this with a favourable eye." What do you mean there?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. That -- there must have been a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well Mr. Kljuic, it's precisely what you're recorded as having said. It's at page 34 -- you don't have this page, but for everybody else, it's at page 34, line 18: "Before the establishment, I don't know which documents he worked on, probably on the Statute, but Mr. Karadzic did not regard this with a favourable eye. Later on, when he was -- later on, as Speaker of parliament, Mr. Krajisnik worked on all the key documents." Now, what -- Mr. Kljuic, if you wish to correct that answer, please do so first.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Mr. Karadzic did not have the ability to deal with that -- he did not -- he wasn't inclined to that sort of work because he was interested in politics and he dealt with politics, whereas the drafting of the Statute requires some sort of an ability to do such work. I never said that Karadzic and Krajisnik were at odds in this respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, so just to clarify then, you're saying your answer wasn't intended to suggest that Mr. Karadzic had any objection to Mr. Krajisnik working on such a document. That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not challenging that explanation, Your Honour, which I just say straight away that I acknowledge that Mr. Kljuic's explanation there is reasonable on his previous answer. When I do challenge his previous answers, then obviously I will do, clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, whatever it was, Mr. Krajisnik was -- Mr. Krajisnik was not a lawyer, was he or is he? Correct?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he has a degree in economics and he held a very high position in the industrial sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I have a degree in economics but I'm a lawyer. The answer is no, he is not a lawyer. Correct? You agree? I'm just trying to get that straight; it's a simple point. You know that, don't you, that Mr. Krajisnik is not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there lawyers in the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, this work by Mr. Krajisnik on any documents - let's get it clear - you have absolutely no knowledge at all, do you, of any work by Mr. Krajisnik on any documents relating to the SDS before its foundation in July 1990.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never really said that I do have information about it, that I know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meetings that you described then, interparty meetings between August 1990 and the election in November 1990, you say, do you, that Mr. Krajisnik was present at at least some of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many such meetings were there during that period, August to November 1990?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many, but there were several.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, we're in the same territory we were last September. I know, or I accept, Mr. Kljuic, that often such estimates will have to be only that and that you may very well not be able to say there were nine meetings or seven meetings, but we had a lot of exchange in September about very loose words like "several." So as best you can estimate with a number rather than a word, how many such meetings do you say there were between August and November 1990?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. There were days when two meetings were held depending on the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's perfectly clear that you do not know an exact number. No one asks an exact number. What we're asking is the fairest estimate you could make of the numbers of meetings in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you allow Mr. Stewart to put to me questions about a number, and then when I give an approximate number, I have to substantiate it. I could tell you, of course, that I had hundreds of meetings with Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just answer the question. If there were hundreds, tell us that there were hundreds, which I take then to be anything between 100 and 200 or 300. If you say there were approximately 20, I will understand that there is most likely between 15 and 25. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that there were 10 meetings where we were -- where there were two parties, the HDZ and the SDS, or where there were all three parties, HDZ, SDS, and SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And an estimated number, Mr. Kljuic, please, only? How many of those meetings do you say were attended by Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only referring to those meetings where I believed Mr. Krajisnik was present as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kljuic, I wasn't. My question -- you referred to these interparty meetings. I did not qualify by reference to Mr. Krajisnik's presence. I asked you how many such meetings. So including -- I'll have you ask you again then, Mr. Kljuic, including all these meetings, how many estimated number during that period, August to November 1990?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, just to make it quite simple: Interparty meetings, Mr. Krajisnik present, you said approximately 10. Yes? Interparty meetings Mr. Krajisnik not being present in that period of time, how many, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to explain something first in order for you to understand me. We had daily contacts between Karadzic, Izetbegovic, Jure Pelivan and myself. Now, the question is what do you consider to be an official meeting, and what is a meeting when we sit at a desk and have coffee together and discuss issues, what it is to be called because the latter types of meetings were more frequent. There were meetings where we were one on one, there were meetings when we were talking about the elections, what sort of joint statements we would make, and of such meetings, there were perhaps 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And of that kind of meetings, but now without Mr. Krajisnik present, interparty meetings where you would make joint statements of the meetings, that seems to be rather formal meetings, how many of them without Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpertation] Of meetings between Karadzic and myself, there were a much greater number as well as of working groups. That is, there was a larger number of working groups. But you have to see what the atmosphere was that prevailed in the period of the collapse of communism when they were allowing political parties for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell us first how many approximately of those relatively formal meetings, as you described them, of which there were 10 with Mr. Krajisnik present and how many were there of similar meetings approximately Mr. Krajisnik not being present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Of official meetings of delegations not attended by Mr. Krajisnik, there were only a few. And as for official contacts between individuals from the SDS and the HDZ, there were very many of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would those very many be the ones Mr. Krajisnik present or Mr. Krajisnik not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do specifically recall 10 of these relatively formal meetings between August and November 1990 at which Mr. Krajisnik was present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kljuic, I put it to you that is just wrong, that Mr. Krajisnik did not attend such meetings at which you were present during that period. I'm asking you to agree or disagree with that proposition I just put to you.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear gentlemen, I have come here on the basis of a law signed between my country and the Tribunal. It is my civic duty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, the question put to you is quite simple. You gave an answer of 10 of those meetings. Mr. Stewart says it's the position of the Defence that this is not a true answer. Do you agree or do you not agree? It's quite simple.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, you first asked me to give you an approximate estimate so I said it was approximately 10. Now you are strictly saying was not 10. What would I have to do? Seek out witnesses. There were very few witnesses attending those meetings. I do not claim that there were 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, the only question put to you is whether the answer you gave was with all the approximation in it, whether it was a correct answer. You answered the question; Defence says it's not the right answer. You agree or you disagree; it's as simple as that. I take it from what you said until now that you disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That was asked to you two minutes ago. If you would just have said, "I disagree with you." That would be enough. Yes? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you're referring to your civic duty. Can I understand, is it your -- you're regarding it as your civic duty, are you, to come to this Tribunal, give this Tribunal all the help you reasonably can in relation to the facts relating to Mr. Krajisnik's case, and to tell the truth? Is that a fair summary what you regard as your civic duty?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is not only in respect of Mr. Krajisnik. I have been in this capacity in regard to a number of cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And specifically in relation to this case where Mr. Krajisnik is on trial, you regard it as your duty to give all the help you reasonably can to get to the truth; correct? You're nodding. Please say yes.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if all the help you reasonably can includes requests to you to provide documents that anybody involved in this case might regard as relevant, then you would loyally and conscientiously comply with that request, would you?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: We solved this last time, you know. Although this does invade my privacy, I did agree to disclose the documents that I have in my possession. What other documents do you want from me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm just wanting to get clear, Mr. Kljuic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the matter of the documents does not need any revisiting at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have a short submission in relation to that, Your Honour, but it will wait rather than inconvenience everybody with inviting the witness to be taken out of court. But I would like just to reserve that I do have a very short submission in relation to the reason for that question. But it will wait, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Kljuic, you're recorded by yourself, as it happens, in relation to Mr. Karadzic as saying: "I simply cannot explain but I had a special kind of superiority over Karadzic. It exactly corresponded to a superiority that a gentleman from the city would have over a little peasant from the Dermitor mountain." They're quite graphic. Do you agree that those are your own words, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If Your Honour -- counsel could direct us to the page in the transcript or another reference, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's actually in one of the documents which was supplied by Mr. Kljuic to the Tribunal since the last hearing. I've got it as a number 15, but then that may be simply the numbering in the note I've been given. It's been described as it's a -- it's four pages of typewritten material. Your Honour, I don't have copies of all this right now but it's one of Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's helpful, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good, I'm always delighted to help. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So we could find it, Your Honour, easily, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, first of all, do you agree that -- accept or agree that those are your own words?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stand by them, do you?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in those -- any meetings or discussions you had with Dr. Karadzic between August and November 1990, did you convey to him or did you hide that feeling of superiority?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should I hide it from Mr. Karadzic seeing that we had known each other for between 25 and 30 years? Mr. Karadzic was, a priori, against any kind of a Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on a number of times he tried to get my involved in such a conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, did you feel a similar special kind of superiority over Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, is, of course, not by any possible factual basis a little peasant from the Dermitor mountain. But leaving that aside, have you felt and do you feel any intellectual superiority over Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We are two totally different persons. And another thing: In our communication, in our interchanges, Mr. Krajisnik was always very correct, which was not the case with Karadzic. And thirdly, with Mr. Krajisnik, we never discussed the subjects that we discussed with Karadzic. I, in fact, think that, formally observed, our relations were very correct, apart from the several key meetings where we disagreed on the issue of the general policy to be pursued in respect of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say in that last bit of that answer that you think that "formally observed, our relations were very correct," you're talking about the relations between you and Mr. Krajisnik, are you, there?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we understand that you do not take the view that your relations with Dr. Karadzic were very correct?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you that Mr. Karadzic's behaviour was very often infantile, rude, and needless to say, as such, it necessarily elicited a reaction on my part. He would say, "There will be no Bosnia and Herzegovina. We shall kill you all." And then I would tell him, "No, there will be a Bosnia and Herzegovina as it has existed up until now." And this is the way in which I had to talk to Mr. Karadzic. With Mr. Krajisnik, I did not have that kind of relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I'm going to try and English phrase and see if it comes across to you in with an appropriate meaning in your own language. Did Dr. Karadzic have a tendency to shoot from the hip? Does that come across as a clear question?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Kljuic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way. You could put it that way. But Mr. Karadzic did not have a vision of a "denouement" regarding the future of Yugoslavia, or the future of Yugoslavia. For instance, he would not adopt -- accept the norms of the Helsinki Conference, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was the word that came across in English "denouement"? I think that's rather a question to the interpreters, Your Honour. That's what I thought I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters are invited, the missing part on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is the word, "denouement," the unravelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a wonderful French word, and I just wanted to check that that was incorporated in that English sentence.
